title: Love without pretending (Romans 12:9–21)
hookLine: rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep; overcome evil with good

cards: A friend texts: I got the job! And in the chest of the person reading it, just for a second, something can tighten. They wanted that kind of news.

They type back: so happy for you!!! with three exclamation points, and they mean it, mostly. Or someone they can't stand has a terrible week, and a small, ugly part of them feels something that isn't quite sympathy.
Love is easy to perform. The emojis are right there. Now Paul gets practical: a list of short commands, almost like a text thread.
The first one is about pretending.

teach.h: A HYPOCRITE WAS AN ACTOR IN A MASK.
teach.b: The first line, in the King James Bible: "Let love be without dissimulation." Dissimulation is an old word for pretending. The Greek is anupokritos: without hypocrisy.
A hypokrites, in Greek, was an actor, someone speaking from behind a stage mask. Paul's point: let love take off the mask. Then the rapid list.
Hate what is evil, hold on to what is good. Outdo one another in showing honor. Be patient in trouble.
Keep praying. Share with those in need. Welcome strangers.

teach.h: REJOICE WITH THEM THAT DO REJOICE.
teach.b: Then two harder lines: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep."

Some readers say the weeping is the easier of the two, and that rejoicing with someone whose good news stings is where the mask really comes off. Then Paul turns to enemies. Bless those who persecute you.
Don't pay back evil for evil.

teach.h: AS MUCH AS LIETH IN YOU.
teach.b: If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men. As much as depends on you, because sometimes it doesn't. Leave vengeance to God.

teach.h: FEED YOUR ENEMY: COALS OF FIRE.
teach.b: Then, quoting Proverbs: "Therefore if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head."

Coals of fire sounds like revenge, but some readers hear it as the burning shame of being treated kindly by someone you've wronged, the kind that might change a heart. Nobody's completely sure where the image comes from.
The chapter ends: "Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good." You can hear Jesus's own teaching behind it: love your enemies, bless those who curse you.

how: Romans 12:9–21 is sometimes read at weddings and taught as a picture of everyday Christian love; some Christians try to live out "overcome evil with good" by answering wrongs with kindness.

o: sincere, with no actor's mask on
so strong it never gets angry
loud and showy, so everyone can see it

games.q: what's inside the list — tap the pairs.

s: heaping coals of fire on someone's head means getting revenge
some readers hear the burning shame of being treated kindly, which might change a heart. the image's origin is uncertain.
the Greek word for hypocrite was also the word for a stage actor
someone speaking behind a mask. Paul's love has no mask.
Paul says you must be at peace with everyone no matter what
"if it be possible, as much as lieth in you." sometimes it doesn't depend on you.

games.q: someone who has wronged you is hungry and has nothing. you have food. what does Paul say to do?
games.why: "if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink." then: "be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good."

practice: Think of someone who has good news right now, a promotion, a baby, a trip, a new love, a win, and if there's a little tightness, notice it honestly; that's all right.
Picture their face when they got the news, and let yourself be glad with them, really glad, as if their good news were partly yours. If you pray, you can thank God for their joy, by name.

wordCard.voice: Anupokritos. Paul's Greek word for love without hypocrisy: no actor's mask, glad with the glad, sad with the sad.

orig.note: Greek: without hypocrisy, unmasked. from hypokritēs, a stage actor.

carryVoice: Your line: overcome evil with good. Real love doesn't need a mask. Until tomorrow, friend.
